extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, and scholars in philosophy of mathematics and foundations of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: A broad, authoritative encyclopedia overview of central positions, problems, and methodological standards in the philosophy of mathematics and foundations (logicism, intuitionism, formalism, predicativism, platonism, structuralism, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Logicism / neo-logicism (reduction to logic)
rubrics_metrics.description: The project of attempting to reduce mathematics to logic; mathematics is 'logic in disguise'. Neo-logicism revives this via abstraction principles such as Hume's Principle, aiming to derive arithmetic from logical principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frege's Basic Law V originally attempted to ground arithmetic but led to inconsistency (Russell's paradox). A successful logicist account must avoid such inconsistent principles; Hume's Principle can be used to derive second-order Peano Arithmetic without Basic Law V. Philosophers now study which abstraction principles are acceptable and why; consistency, the logical status of the principle, and what can be derived from weakened background logics are central concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intuitionism / constructivist requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics is essentially an activity of construction carried out by an ideal mathematician; mathematical existence claims must provide constructive methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-constructive existence proofs (those that assert existence without providing a method to produce an example) are rejected as unacceptable. Intuitionistic logic removes the principle of excluded middle (φ ∨ ¬φ) and related principles (e.g., double negation elimination). The accepted formal theory is weaker (Heyting Arithmetic rather than Peano Arithmetic). This entails a revision of much classical mathematics; translations exist to embed many classical results into intuitionistic frameworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formalism / minimal requirement of consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics consists of formal systems (strings of symbols) manipulated according to rules; a minimal, non-negotiable requirement for such systems is consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On formalist views (Hilbert, Curry, etc.) formal systems are treated instrumentally; inconsistent systems are useless because they prove every statement. Hilbert's program sought to prove consistency of stronger systems in 'safe' weaker systems like arithmetic. Gödel's incompleteness theorems show limitations (consistency of a sufficiently strong system cannot be proved within that system), but formalism can persist by treating systems pragmatically or focusing on arithmetically verifiable parts. Arithmetical soundness and relative consistency proofs remain important guiding standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predicativism / avoidance of impredicative definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions and constructions should be predicative: a definition must not implicitly refer to the totality it defines (the vicious circle principle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impredicative definitions (those violating the vicious circle principle) are considered illegitimate. Predicativism accepts the natural numbers but restricts arbitrary subsets to those definable by first-order (arithmetical) predicates; the predicativist program can be iterated transfinitely along predicative ordinals (Feferman, Schütte). Much of classical analysis can be reconstructed predicatively, but highly impredicative set theory (transfinite set theory) lies outside predicativist acceptability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstraction-principle acceptability
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstraction principles (schemes that introduce objects by equating them when certain equivalences hold, e.g., Hume's Principle or Frege's Basic Law V) must be evaluated for acceptability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criteria include logical status (is the principle genuine logic?), consistency with background theory, and what mathematical strength the principle yields. Basic Law V is inconsistent in full second-order logic (hence unacceptable), while Hume's Principle appears consistent and can yield arithmetic. Philosophers attempt to develop general theories explaining which abstraction principles are acceptable and why; weaker background theories can sometimes recuperate otherwise problematic principles at the cost of deriving weaker mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accepting axioms: intrinsic vs extrinsic evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Axioms may be supported either by intrinsic evidence (mathematical intuition) or by extrinsic evidence (fruitfulness and success in yielding verifiable consequences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gödel emphasized intrinsic mathematical intuition as evidence for axioms (e.g., ZFC), but also allowed extrinsic evidence: new axioms may be accepted if they are fruitful, simplify proofs, produce verifiable consequences, and shed light across a field. Extrinsic success—especially verifiable consequences and explanatory power—can justify accepting axioms even if intrinsic intuition is lacking. This is central in debates about new set-theoretic axioms and the continuum hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalism / indispensability criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical entities are to be accepted ontologically to the extent they are indispensable to our best scientific theories; philosophy should consult scientific practice (Quinean naturalism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quinean confirmational holism and Putnam's application argue that because scientific theories are mathematically formulated, mathematics used indispensably in these theories is empirically confirmed. Thus ontology should include the mathematical entities indispensable to science. Counterarguments emphasize that the mathematics used may be predicatively reducible or that mathematicians' practices impose different standards; naturalism remains a methodological standard for some philosophers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maddy's methodological maxims: 'unify' and 'maximize'
rubrics_metrics.description: Set-theoretic methodological maxims guiding acceptability of principles: 'unify' (seek a single system instantiating mathematical objects/structures) and 'maximize' (adopt powerful, mathematically fruitful principles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These maxims are invoked by philosophers (Maddy) as standards set theorists implicitly use when considering the acceptability of new set-theoretic principles. 'Unify' favors axioms that allow broad instantiation of mathematical structures; 'maximize' favors strong, fruitful axioms. They are heuristic methodological criteria rather than formal rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deflationary/internalist criterion (Carnap/Tait)
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions about mathematical existence and truth should be asked and answered within mathematical frameworks (internal questions); external metaphysical questions are insoluble or misguided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnap's internal/external distinction and Tait's application suggest that ontological questions only make sense relative to a chosen axiomatic framework; philosophers should 'let mathematics speak for itself' and avoid seeking supramathematical metaphysical grounding. This deflationary stance is presented as a methodological alternative to platonistic metaphysics and is defended by appealing to mathematical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistemological adequacy / Benacerraf's epistemological problem
rubrics_metrics.description: A satisfactory philosophy of mathematics must explain how mathematicians have epistemic access to mathematical entities and obtain knowledge of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benacerraf's argument challenges platonism by noting that standard causal or reliabilist accounts of knowledge struggle to explain knowledge of non-spatiotemporal abstract objects. Any position that posits abstract mathematical entities must address how reliable belief and reference to such entities are possible (Hodes' semantic variant emphasizes reference conditions). Failure to provide an epistemic account is an important objection against ontologies of mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plenitudinous platonism (ontological criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine that every logically consistent mathematical theory refers to an abstract entity; the mere entertaining of a consistent theory confers reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plenitudinous platonism is advanced as a way to solve epistemological problems by positing that consistent theories automatically secure reference to abstract objects. It is controversial and raises questions about how to handle consistency, individuation of objects, and epistemic access; proponents include Linsky & Zalta and Balaguer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good mathematical proof: explanatory and understanding value
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'good' mathematical proof should do more than establish truth; it should explain why a statement holds and contribute to mathematical understanding by revealing deep relations among concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophers and mathematicians often judge proofs not merely by verification but by explanatory depth: linking different domains, showing conceptual reasons for results, and providing insight. Computer-assisted proofs often succeed at verification but are criticized for lacking explanatory power, being low-level, and failing to develop or link deep concepts; this motivates philosophical inquiry into the nature of mathematical understanding and standards for acceptable proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for computer-assisted proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation criteria for computer proofs focus on reliability, the level of conceptual development achieved, and the provision of understanding beyond mere verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Computer proofs are typically strong at checking low-level combinatorial cases but weaker at producing deep conceptual explanations or linking disparate fields. Philosophical concerns include assessing the reliability of automated inference, whether such proofs can yield a priori knowledge, and what counts as acceptable explanation. Debates consider whether additional standards (e.g., reproducibility, human-checkable high-level explanations) should be required for acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of inconsistent principles / ensuring consistent background theories
rubrics_metrics.description: One must avoid adopting principles that lead to paradoxes or contradictions (e.g., Frege's Basic Law V); where problematic principles are used, one should work in weakened background theories that render them consistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The history of foundations shows the destructive impact of inconsistent principles. Acceptability demands attention to consistency proofs, restrictions (typing, weakening second-order logic), or understanding the limited arithmetical strength derivable in weakened settings. The anti-pattern is relying on apparently intuitive but inconsistent axioms without checking consistency implications.
